section.title: Operate, investigate, and stay grounded in how systems work
section.deck: Marc Brooker connects customer needs, incident learning, database design, writing, and hands-on adaptation to the work of an influential engineer.

blocks.question: How do you find the problems that matter most?
answer: Brooker recommends looking broadly rather than optimizing only the volume of one’s own code. Customers reveal work they find difficult, investments they are making, and operational chores they wish did not distract from their businesses. Technical trends supply another input: faster networks, storage, compute, multicore systems, and GPUs can make previously impractical designs possible. Changes in the wider world create openings too.

He gives a concrete collision of those inputs. While working with Lambda customers in 2020, he heard enthusiasm for serverless and containers but dissatisfaction with how operationally server-oriented relational databases fit those workloads. Moving to Aurora let him help address that mismatch. He also describes using an object store as a database durability foundation while adding architecture to supply latency and interfaces suited to online workloads. Customer needs and changes in technical economics together explained why the product could matter.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: Why remain on call for so many years?
answer: He sees on-call work and deep incident analysis as the source of much of his practical distributed-systems knowledge. Strong programming, mathematics, and computer-science foundations do not automatically teach how customers actually use a running system, how unexpected use changes its behavior, or how to make it resilient.

This is not praise for repeatedly closing identical tickets. Automate rote work. The valuable part is investigating unusual behavior, understanding it, improving the system, and sharing the lesson. He describes a broad weekly AWS meeting where engineers and leaders examine correction-of-error reports together and apply their lessons across services.

Leadership attention to operational reality helps guide product and architecture decisions. Repeated failures may expose a need for a common tool, library, service, or feature rather than another local patch. Brooker estimates having read between three and four thousand internal and industry postmortems over his career; even small lessons accumulate.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: What makes a good postmortem?
answer: Begin by understanding what actually happened, rather than fitting the event to an existing bias. If that is impossible, the difficulty itself identifies missing observability, logging, metrics, or simulation capability. Then examine causes at several levels: the code defect, why testing missed it, why the testing approach or assumptions were inadequate, and which team or organizational decisions shaped those conditions.

A useful report must neither stop at the nearest defect nor dissolve into the vague conclusion that failures happen. It needs concrete actions at the relevant levels. Looking across reports can reveal whole classes of problems worth addressing with a shared mechanism.

While designing Aurora DSQL, the team studied recurring relational-database incidents. One pattern was a distributed client opening a transaction and then disappearing because of garbage collection, connectivity loss, or another pause while continuing to hold locks. The design question became how to prevent that whole failure class for customers, rather than only repair each incident.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: How can a database avoid trouble from a client that stops mid-transaction?
answer: In the DSQL design he describes, reads use multiversion concurrency control rather than pessimistic locking. Rows have historical versions, so readers can read an appropriate version without preventing writers from updating it. Writes are accumulated locally in the query processor and checked optimistically at commit time.

This prevents a stalled reader from locking out writers and prevents uncommitted writing from blocking readers. Brooker corrects his own wording about writers: one writer does not hold a blocking lock over another, but conflicting changes can cause another transaction to fail its eventual commit check. That limitation follows from the required isolation semantics rather than the abandoned-client lock problem.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

followups.question: How much storage overhead does keeping old versions introduce?
answer: He says it depends strongly on workload but is often smaller than expected. Updates tend to concentrate on a small portion of rows; an active row may acquire many versions while most data stays unchanged. In his experience it is unusual for an online workload’s version-retention storage overhead to exceed roughly ten percent. He does not present that figure as an unconditional sizing rule.
followups.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: Why should a team with weak postmortem habits invest in them?
answer: The choice is where to spend engineering time: improving the product or fighting the same fire repeatedly. A weak culture may lack a sufficiently clear focus on outcomes and customer experience. Standards need not be identical everywhere; durability-critical systems deserve especially high standards, while another product may deliberately accept more defects to optimize other goals. The important distinction is an intentional tradeoff.

Another failure mode is normalizing operational heroics. A team that stays up all night, tolerates constant pages, and fixes every emergency may feel admirable from inside, yet spend its strongest ownership and expertise on an expensive repeating break-fix cycle. The corrective move is to redirect that energy into understanding and removing causes. Preventing recurrence creates time for deeper product improvements.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: Why is adding a cache sometimes a poor distributed-system design choice?
answer: Caching exploits locality and can improve speed and scale. Its danger is the difference between modes: a warm cache containing the right data is fast, but an empty or unsuitable cache sends demand to a backend that may be unable to handle it. Overload can then prevent refilling the cache, leaving the system stably unhealthy instead of naturally recovering. Brooker calls that a metastable failure.

He gives two ways to reduce the mode change. DSQL’s storage tier holds a complete copy of the data, avoiding an empty-working-set recovery problem. Aurora continually tells potential failover targets what to cache so the new leader begins warm. Other options include a complete local materialized view for slow-changing data or a backend that provides the required scale directly.

He prefers avoiding caches where feasible but explicitly refuses to make that universal. The lesson is to understand recovery behavior and dependencies rather than apply “add a cache” as an automatic improvement.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

followups.question: How often do metastable failures occur in practice?
answer: An individual service can run for years without one. Brooker nevertheless believes this mechanism underlies many of the industry’s most severe outages. When it occurs, recovery can be long and complicated and may require painfully stopping and restarting parts of the system. His claim is about the disproportionate importance of rare failure modes, not their being an everyday event.
followups.speaker: Marc Brooker

Contention or saturated resources can prevent refilling.

blocks.question: How do you expect AI to change software engineering?
answer: Brooker begins with uncertainty: these are predictions. He believes software remains supply-constrained and that there is enormous room for more useful, personalized, better-fitting software. Falling development costs therefore excite him rather than implying all useful software has already been built.

He expects the economics of products, organizations, and careers to change, with success depending partly on adapting to and leading that change. He offers no settled timetable; the opportunity and the need to adapt are his central forecast.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: Can someone still succeed using older techniques instead of joining the new mainstream?
answer: He describes three overlapping possibilities. Software craft can remain enjoyable as a hobby even when a method is no longer economically competitive, much as hand-tool joinery or retrocomputing can be worthwhile for pleasure. Older technologies can also support real careers in specialized niches because changing the real world is slow, shaped by policy, people, and organizational constraints.

His analogy is analog electronics: digital became dominant without eliminating valuable specialized work in areas such as radio and power. Nevertheless, he expects the main economic opportunity in software to move toward AI-assisted, agentic, specification-driven, and still-emerging practices that build at different cost and speed. He particularly sees interesting adoption problems where software meets the physical world. He would personally favor that new mainstream while recognizing the other paths.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: What should junior engineers emphasize when generating code becomes easier?
answer: Find problems that matter and understand their context earlier: customers, the business, economics, and the surrounding system. Brooker expects activities once insulated from junior engineers to enter their careers sooner. A role centered exclusively on typing in an IDE for a full day may become harder to sustain.

He also sees opportunity for deep specialists. Scientific, technical, optimization, infrastructure, or database expertise helps a person ask the right questions. Less boilerplate can let that knowledge become useful software or a product with less friction. Understanding customers and developing depth are both valuable routes, not opposing stereotypes.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: What would you say to a new engineer frightened by those higher expectations?
answer: He does not expect a new graduate to know everything immediately. Employers and early-career engineers both benefit from people succeeding, so organizations must build a supported learning path. First customer conversations can be scary; mentorship, feedback, guardrails, and progressively larger experiences make them learnable.

He compares this with other professions where much practical learning occurs on the job. What changes is the emphasis of the learning, not the fact that graduates need it. Leaders must rethink the career ladder rather than simply hire beginners and demand expert performance. He acknowledges uncertainty while remaining optimistic about the scale of opportunity.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: How should senior engineers adapt?
answer: Retain the value of accumulated judgment by returning to hands-on building. A person who influences design without practicing current development methods can become disconnected from what builders actually encounter. Brooker recommends curiosity, direct experience, and humility about how quickly the practice changes.

He argues that newer tools can make limited practitioner time more productive by reducing boilerplate, and that building reconnects engineers with the reasons they entered the field: learning technology and solving customers’ problems. In his conversations, active users offer concrete assessments of tools’ strengths, failures, and missing integrations; nonusers often have poor mental models. That is his observation rather than a categorical verdict on every skeptic.

He also sees the broader lesson in earlier AWS products. Engineers he admired could connect cloud strategy and economics with minute technical details. Grounded leadership helped them make enduring products. The gap between detached advice and implementation is not new, but he thinks fast-changing tools make it larger.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: Why write so much as an engineer?
answer: Writing lets expertise travel across both people and time. A product, individual mentorship, and talks all spread knowledge, but an old written explanation can still help a reader a decade later. He values writing as a multiplier rather than merely as a visibility activity.

It also sharpens the writer’s thought. Putting an idea into prose forces a depth and clarity that speech or slides may not. Brooker sometimes writes with no intention of publishing. He appreciates Leslie Lamport’s stronger case for formal mathematics while seeing prose as an accessible starting point. Sharing ideas, preserving them, and understanding them better are separate but compatible motives.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: What do you say to engineers who see documentation as busy work?
answer: Ask what the writing is for and whether it operates at the right level of the problem. Brooker does not find every design notation useful; he criticizes UML as focusing on a semantic level that did not help his own work. A document can be valuable because it preserves a decision for future readers or helps reason through a difficult, hard-to-reverse design or API choice. Routine, reversible choices do not all warrant the same process.

For important designs, recording the rationale also distinguishes careful decisions from temporary guesses made without data. Future engineers can reconsider arbitrary choices with new evidence while taking more care to understand the reasoning behind deliberate ones. The amount of prior thought matters alongside the result. Writing for that purpose is a skill worth developing even if the activity is not naturally enjoyable.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: How do you balance doing the work with discussing it?
answer: He sees both extremes as failure modes. A deeply capable person who never communicates could have more impact by sharing and could miss important problems by staying inside an IDE. Someone who only talks could make their advice more relevant by returning to practice.

Brooker personally spends roughly seventy-five to eighty percent of his effort practicing and the remainder teaching or communicating. Strong colleagues vary from approximately ninety-ten to fifty-fifty; he offers these as observations rather than an optimal allocation formula. Dedicated communicators can have a different job, provided they remain curious and honest about what they do and do not know. During fast change, he would lean somewhat more toward practice without severing contact with the outside world.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: Is it better to be overrated or underrated?
answer: For the long term, he would choose underrated. Being overrated may feel good but is difficult to sustain. Sports and crafts expose the gap between appearance and capability quickly; engineering can leave room for qualitative perceptions longer. The careers he admires are built on honesty about actual knowledge and skill, not on maintaining an inflated image. This complements his recommendation to communicate useful expertise rather than hide it.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: Which AWS engineers do you admire, and why?
answer: He highlights retired colleague Al Vermeulen, whose work included major contributions to S3 and database design. Brooker remembers debating fine points of Paxos with him around 2010 while also seeing him discuss executive-level cloud strategy and explain what the business should build. He admired the ability to move across those levels without losing depth.
More generally, he respects colleagues motivated by useful work and customer impact rather than celebrity. Breadth, detail, and purpose together form the example he wants to follow.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: What technical reading do you recommend?
answer: He recommends Martin Kleppmann’s distributed-systems book and Hennessy and Patterson’s computer-architecture book. The captions contain an initial imprecise reference to the latter followed by his correction; the intended authors and subject are retained without reconstructing a full title. His comment about a forthcoming edition belongs to the interview’s time context.

For his own technical learning he reads many papers. He sometimes uses an AI summary to get oriented before reading the authors’ actual words; the summary is a bridge into the source. Old work also contains valuable insights. He describes Lambda traffic-management ideas drawing on Erlang’s much older work on telephone systems. Rapid industry change does not make foundational research obsolete.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker

blocks.question: What advice would you give yourself when first joining AWS?
answer: Be a little bolder about moving when learning and impact begin to taper. He loved his early teams in EC2 and EBS and was more hesitant to leave than he now thinks ideal. He made about four substantial organizational changes and suspects a few more might have been better, rather than recommending constant movement.

He would repeatedly ask what he is learning, whom he is learning from, and whether another environment would help him learn more quickly. Following curiosity has been both useful and enjoyable in his own career.
blocks.speaker: Marc Brooker
